children.translated_text: Having bowed to the omniscient one who is everything,
with actions of mind, speech, and body,
this work called <s>Kāvyālaṃkāra</s> (Ornament of Poetry)
shall be composed to the best of my understanding.
In <s>dharma</s> (righteousness), <s>artha</s> (wealth), <s>kāma</s> (pleasure), and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation),
discernment, and in the arts —
it produces both delight and fame:
the composition of good poetry.
Like generosity in one who has no wealth,
like skill in weapons in a eunuch,
like boldness in an ignorant person,
so is knowledge of <s>śāstra</s> (treatises) in one who is not a poet.
What is beauty without modesty?
What is night without the moon?
Devoid of true poetic skill,
what kind of eloquence can there be?
Through a teacher's instruction, even the dull-witted
are capable of studying <s>śāstra</s> (treatises);
but poetry is born only
in one who possesses <s>pratibhā</s> (creative genius).
Even of those who have ascended to heaven,
of those who were creators of compositions,
there remains without decay
a beautiful body made of poetry.
And his imperishable fame fills
both heaven and earth;
for so long does this meritorious one
occupy the realm of the gods.
Therefore, one who desires fame
more enduring than earthly existence
should make effort, having understood what is to be known,
in the characteristics of poetry.
Words, metre, denotation and meaning,
narratives based on <s>itihāsa</s> (traditional history),
worldly experience, reasoning, and the arts —
these should be regarded as the sources of poetry.

children.translated_text: Having learned what words denote,
having devoted oneself to those who know,
and having examined the compositions of others,
one should undertake the practice of poetry with care.
Not even a single word should ever
be uttered if it is faulty,
for one is reproached by a bad poem
as by a wicked son — bringing disgrace.
Lack of poetic skill does not lead to <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness),
nor to disease, nor to punishment;
but bad poetry, the wise declare,
is verily death itself.
<s>Rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and other <s>alaṃkāras</s> (ornaments)
of poetry have been described in many ways by others;
even a beautiful woman's face does not shine
without ornaments.
Others call <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and similar figures
external ornaments,
and desire the derivation of nominal and verbal forms
to be the true ornament of speech.
They call this grammatical correctness;
but propriety of meaning is not of this kind alone.
The twofold division into ornament of word
and ornament of sense — that is our doctrine.
Word and meaning together constitute <s>kāvya</s> (poetry),
and that is of two kinds: prose and verse.
<s>Saṃskṛta</s> (Sanskrit), <s>Prākṛta</s> (Prakrit),
and <s>Apabhraṃśa</s> — thus it is threefold.
It narrates events that have occurred,
and also invented subject matter,
and that which is based on arts and sciences —
thus it is further divided into four kinds.
<s>Sargabandha</s> (canto-composition), works meant for dramatic performance,
likewise <s>ākhyāyikā</s> (romance) and <s>kathā</s> (tale),
and unbound poetry —
these are again said to be fivefold.
<s>Sargabandha</s> is <s>mahākāvya</s> (great poem) —
that which is great and concerns great persons,
which has refined (non-vulgar) words and meaningful content,
is endowed with <s>alaṃkāras</s> (ornaments), and has a worthy subject.
That which is furnished with counsels, embassies, marches, battles,
and the triumph of the hero,
joined with the five <s>sandhis</s> (junctures of plot),
not overly verbose, and rich in content,

children.translated_text: even when treating all four aims of life,
chiefly serves to instruct in <s>artha</s> (practical purpose),
is consistent with the nature of the world,
and employs all the <s>rasas</s> (aesthetic sentiments) severally,
having first introduced the hero
through his lineage, valor, learning, and so forth —
one should not describe his death,
out of a desire to glorify another.
If he is not accepted as pervading
the body of the poem,
then for one who partakes of good fortune,
praise and invocation at the beginning are pointless.
<s>Nāṭaka</s> (drama), <s>dvipadī</s>, <s>śamyā</s>,
<s>rāsaka</s>, <s>skandhaka</s>, and the like —
these are said to be meant for dramatic performance;
their elaboration has been stated by others.
With Sanskrit that is clear to the ear, unconfused,
with proper words, meanings, phrases, and style,
composed in prose with elevated and noble meaning,
divided into <s>ucchvāsas</s> (chapters) — that is deemed an <s>ākhyāyikā</s> (romance).
In it, what is narrated is the hero's
own deeds, told by himself;
it has <s>vaktra</s> (direct narration) and <s>aparavaktra</s> (indirect narration),
and passages that indicate future events at the proper time.
It is marked by certain narrations
composed according to the poet's intention,
and is furnished with the abduction of a maiden, battle,
separation, and final union.
That which is not furnished with <s>vaktra</s> and <s>aparavaktra</s>,
nor divided into <s>ucchvāsas</s> (chapters),
whether in Sanskrit or non-Sanskrit,
is a <s>kathā</s> (tale), and may also partake of <s>Apabhraṃśa</s>.
In a <s>kathā</s>, the hero's own story
is narrated by others, not by himself;
how could a person of noble birth
display his own virtues?
Unbound poetry, again, consists of <s>gāthā</s> (verse),
<s>śloka</s>, <s>mātrā</s>, and the like;
endowed with <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) and <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description),
all of this is considered desirable.
Some wise persons hold that
there exists something other called <s>Vaidarbha</s> (the Vidarbha style),
and that it alone is superior,
even if meaningful — not the other.
This is <s>Gauḍīya</s> (the Gauḍa style),
that is <s>Vaidarbha</s> — why this distinction?
Following convention blindly,
the unintelligent should not make such pronouncements.
Now, what belongs to the <s>Aśmaka</s> lineage and such
is called <s>Vaidarbha</s> —
let it be so if you wish; generally
nomenclature is established by convention.
That which has lean meaning, lacks <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression),
is clear, straightforward, and soft,
is different — it is like a song,
merely pleasant to the ear.
Endowed with <s>alaṃkāras</s> (ornaments), free from vulgarity,
meaningful, logically sound, and unconfused —
even <s>Gauḍīya</s> (Gauḍa style) that is excellent
is <s>Vaidarbha</s> — it is not otherwise.
Charm of speech is not produced
by excessive smoothness alone;
<s>Vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) — indirect expression of word and meaning —
is the desired ornament of speech.
That which requires interpretation, is strained, means something else,
is non-denotative, or logically unsound,
or employs obscure words —
poets do not use such expressions.
That is called <s>neyārtha</s> (requiring interpretation) whose meaning
is forced by learned ones with effort,
not established by the natural convention of words,
but somehow through their own intention.
As in '<s>māyā</s> eva <s>bhadrā</s>' (illusion itself is auspicious) —
that is an improper construction;
and '<s>veṇudāke</s>' and the like —
they force such meanings without verbal warrant.

children.translated_text: That which is logically unsound — as when messengers are
clouds, winds, and the moon,
or likewise bees, <s>hārīta</s> birds,
<s>cakravāka</s> birds, parrots, and the like.
Those that are speechless or have inarticulate speech,
and wander in distant lands —
how could they undertake the task of a messenger?
This is not justified by reason.
If it is argued that one speaks thus
out of longing, as if mad,
let it be so — but this convention
is employed extensively by the wise.
The use of obscure words
should not be employed under any circumstance;
even for the learned, such usage
does not serve any purpose.

children.translated_text: Faults of sound, faults of meaning,
faults of construction, and also
harshness of sound — thus the wise declare
a fourfold classification of verbal defects.
Words containing sounds suggestive of excrement, filth, vomit,
cutting, wetness, and similar associations,
or suggesting assault, belching,
emission, and bodily functions,
'<s>hiraṇyaretāḥ</s>' (golden semen), '<s>sambādha</s>' (constriction),
'<s>pelava</s>' (soft/flaccid), '<s>upasthita</s>' (approached), '<s>aṇḍaja</s>' (egg-born),
'<s>vākkāṭa</s>' and the like —
these are regarded as words faulty to the ear.
A fault of meaning, on the other hand, should be recognized
as that where, upon being spoken, there arises an understanding
pertaining to unseemly subject matter,
as with words that denote such things.
Of one who has set out to kill,
who is rigid, seeking an opening —
'falling' necessarily occurs,
and recovery comes only with difficulty.
When in the joining of two words
an undesirable meaning is produced,
that is called a fault of construction —
as in '<s>sa śauryābharaṇaḥ</s>' (he whose ornament is valor / he is bereft of valor).
Such as '<s>ajihlada</s>' and the like —
that is known as harshness of sound;
the skilled do not desire it,
and some even reject the <s>gaṇḍa</s> (cluster of harsh sounds).
Yet through a particular arrangement,
even a faulty expression may look beautiful,
like a blue <s>palāśa</s> (Butea) flower placed
between flowers in a garland.
Through the beauty of its setting,
even something improper acquires charm,
like dark collyrium placed
upon a beautiful woman's eyes.
'Your face, O lotus-eyed one,
has cheeks that are pale' —
through the combination with the word '<s>pāṇḍu</s>' (pale),
the word '<s>gaṇḍa</s>' (cheek) is used appropriately, as stated.
By this same principle, one should understand that
even an improper usage may be fitting;
as with elephants whose cheeks
are moist with <s>mada</s> (rut-fluid) —
'of elephants whose temples are wet with rut-fluid,
four hundred <s>dvirada</s> (elephants)' —
thus, as in that example, what is less proper
and what is more proper should both be employed.

children.translated_text: just as a garland-maker, knowing well, fashions a garland,
so should expression in poetry be arranged by one of attentive mind.
Thus ends the first chapter of <s>Bhāmaha</s>'s <s>Alaṃkāra</s>.
Second chapter.
One who desires <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness)
and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity), being wise,
should not employ words with many
compounds.
Some, wishing to express <s>ojas</s> (vigor),
compound many words together,
as in '<s>mandārakusuma-</s>
<s>reṇupiñjaritālakā</s>' (she whose locks are yellowed by the pollen of <s>mandāra</s> flowers).
Poetry that does not have excessively compounded meaning
and is pleasant to hear is considered sweet,
whose meaning is understood by all — from the learned
to women and children — and possesses <s>prasāda</s> (clarity).
<s>Anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>yamaka</s> (rhyme/repetition),
<s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination), and <s>upamā</s> (simile) —
these are the ornaments of speech,
enumerated as five by others.
The arrangement of similar-sounding syllables
is called <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration),
as in '<s>kiṃ tayā cintayā kānte</s>
<s>nitāntā</s>' — as has been stated.
Some wise persons, however, consider other types
to be vulgar <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration),
as in '<s>sa lolamālānīlāli-</s>
<s>kulākulagalo balaḥ</s>' — [excessive alliteration].
<s>Anuprāsas</s> (alliterations) that bear different meanings
and do not use dissimilar syllables,
following this middle path,
produce charming speech.
Some also consider <s>Lāṭīya</s> (the Lāṭa type)
to be an <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), as in:
'Cast your gaze that is a delight to the eyes' —
said the moon to the moon-faced one.
<s>Yamaka</s> (repetition) at the beginning, middle, and end,
<s>pādābhyāsa</s> (repetition of quarter-verses), and <s>āvalī</s> (series),
<s>yamaka</s> of entire quarter-verses —
thus it is said to be fivefold.
<s>Sandaṣṭaka</s> (interlocking), <s>samudga</s> (casket), and the like
are considered included within these;
it may occur at the beginning, or at the middle and end —
thus there are only five types. For example:
'By that good man, by that good man,
the royal one, the royal one, maintained —
to unite what is united,
to bring together people who are assembled.'
The virtuous one, fearing this <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of existence) which is essenceless,
having ended his afflictions, treads the path of tranquility;
the birth of diseases, uncontrollable and unsubdued —
desiring what is better, O you, cut them off, O you who are liberated.

children.translated_text: 'Your mind, O steadfast one, does not dwell
on delightful pleasures;
yet these <s>ramaṇī</s> (beautiful women) captivate
even sages in whose company they are.'
Her of dark and fair eyes, of beautiful breasts and lips,
full of intoxication, with manifest passion, a crest-jewel of beauty,
dense as clouds, dark as clouds, with cloud-dark tresses —
they make my beloved restless, and they depart.
These kings, who have been granted full sovereignty,
whose commands are never obstructed,
who punish the guilty and those who violate the path,
who occupy such thrones inherited from their fathers —
In adjacent and alternate quarter-verses,
and likewise at the ends of quarter-verses,
and throughout all quarter-verses completely —
such [<s>yamaka</s>] is difficult to achieve well.
The repetition of syllables that sound alike
but differ in their meanings
from one another —
that is called <s>yamaka</s> (repetition).
That which uses well-known words, is vigorous,
has well-joined word-compounds,
is clear and has proper expression —
such <s>yamaka</s> is approved by the skilled.
That which is deep with various verbal root meanings,
and is designated as <s>yamaka</s> —
that is called a <s>prahelikā</s> (riddle),
as in '<s>Rāmaśarmācyutottare</s>' (<s>Rāma</s>, <s>Śarma</s>, <s>Acyuta</s> in sequence).
If these poetic works too
are comprehensible only through commentary, like <s>śāstras</s> (treatises),
they are a feast only for the learned —
alas, the dull-witted are undone!
When the nature of the object of comparison
is identified with the standard of comparison,
seeing the equality of qualities —
that is known as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor).
Pertaining to the entire object,
or varying in one aspect —
<s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) is declared to be of two kinds;
this shall now be illustrated.
Producing spray, water, and rut-fluid,
lofty cloud-elephants
come forth, intoxicating —
these elephants restrained by the rainbow.

children.translated_text: Of those whose girths are lightning-girdles,
who bear garlands of <s>balākā</s> (cranes),
the deep rumbling of the rain-clouds
torments that beloved of mine.
Pertaining to the beginning, middle, and end —
<s>dīpaka</s> (illumination) is considered threefold;
because one thing has three states,
it is thus divided into three.
These render its name meaningful,
since it illuminates the meaning;
with three examples, this
is illustrated in three ways, as follows:
Intoxication produces delight
accompanied by passion and the breaking of pride;
it produces longing for union with the beloved,
and unbearable sorrow of the mind.
Spring adorns women
wearing garlands and fine garments;
it adorns the songs of <s>hārīta</s> birds and parrots,
and the foothills of mountains.
The summer heat wishes to bring to an end
the forests with their crickets, the rivers with drying waters,
and the hearts of those who are away from home.
When through a contrary standard of comparison,
by means of place, time, action, and the like,
the similarity of the object of comparison
is established even by a partial quality — that is <s>upamā</s> (simile).
The words '<s>yathā</s>' (as) and '<s>iva</s>' (like) indicate similarity
between things that are different from each other.
dark like a blade of <s>dūrvā</s> grass,
slender like a dark <s>śyāmalā</s> (dark-green) creeper.
Without the words 'as' or 'like' (<s>iva</s>, <s>yathā</s>),
the other type is expressed through a compound,
such as 'lotus-eyed' (<s>kamalapatrākṣī</s>)
or 'moon-faced' (<s>śaśāṅkavadana</s>).
Even with the possessive suffix, when similarity in action is expressed,
it is stated as 'like that' —
'he studies like a twice-born,'
'he teaches us like a teacher.'
Through the placement of a similar subject-matter,
it is called <s>prativastūpamā</s> (counter-subject simile) —
even without explicit statement, as in <s>iva</s>,
from the apprehension of similarity in qualities.
Being-common-to-the-good and such qualities
are what is distinguished here;
that quality produces similarity
even when there is opposition between the two, as:
'How many are there who are virtuous,
sharing the beauty common to the good?
How many mango trees with sweet-ripened fruits
or how many trees along the path?'
As for what some great thinkers have said
about three varieties of simile —
it is here stated through the distinctions
of blame, praise, and desire to describe.
Since the general qualities have been indicated,
all three are already covered.
The garland-simile and all such elaborations
are not superior — expansion is in vain.
Inferiority in occurrence, gender,
difference of expression, reversal,
excess in the standard of comparison,
and also dissimilarity through that —
these are the seven faults of simile
stated by the wise;
with examples and definitions,
they are described here separately.
He, wearing yellow garments agitated by the wind,
holding playfully a lotus of moon-like radiance,
that great hero, grasping the <s>Śārṅga</s> bow,
shone like a cloud with <s>Indra</s>'s rainbow.

children.translated_text: Here, the grasping of <s>Śakra</s>'s (Indra's) bow
is said to show the war-bow,
but since the garment and the conch are not taken up,
it is said to be deficient.
Complete resemblance in every respect
does not exist for any entity;
skillful poets employ similes
as is fitting.
Where is the moon with its unbroken disc,
and where is the radiance of a beloved's face?
Yet because of some general similarity in lustre,
it is compared to the moon.
Moreover, should poems be judged
by the rules of the great ones?
Or has complete resemblance been seen,
as stated in the <s>Rājamitra</s> example?
Among the peacocks, whose eyes were closed by the sun's rays,
dejected, with lotuses free of intoxication due to the wind,
their cries vanished from their mouths,
like virtuous women in their homes bereft of their husbands.

children.translated_text: how can streams of water
from the blazing sun
exist? From this impossibility, by reasoning,

With such an impossible meaning,
what skillful poet would make a simile?
Who indeed would make fire

in both simile and poetic fancy (<s>utprekṣā</s>), as:
'This elephant shines
as if darkness were heaped up;
the lake, with its autumn-clear water,
appears as if a piece of sky were dropped.'

are stated, along with their reversal;
due to inferiority and excess,
each is of two kinds, and all three are illustrated as follows:

of single-minded devotion,
like a river with rough, rock-split waves

children.translated_text: 'Even if the resemblance of elephants and such
to planets is asserted,
still, do they share
either lustre or ferocity?'
Thus the division of simile has been stated;
another further type will be described.
Apart from the ornament of simile,
another distinction is stated.
<s>Ākṣepa</s> (seeming denial), <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration),
<s>vyatireka</s> (contrast), <s>vibhāvanā</s> (causation without cause),
<s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), and <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole) —
these are six other ornaments.
Of these, <s>ākṣepa</s> is considered of two kinds:
pertaining to what is about to be stated and to what has been stated;
the rest will be described
in a single form, in due order.
That which appears like a denial of what is desired
but is meant to convey a distinction —
the learned call it <s>ākṣepa</s> (seeming denial),
and it is of two kinds, as:
'If I were not to see you
even for a moment, I would become anxious;
let this much suffice — what is the use
of saying anything else unpleasant to you?'
'It is no wonder that you are not arrogant,
you whose feet have conquered the earth;
what cause is sufficient
to produce agitation in the ocean?'

children.translated_text: The introduction of another meaning
apart from the one stated —
that should be known as <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration),
which follows the prior meaning, as:
'When you wish to see
the fearsome hostile armies, there is no distress for you;
whether for good or ill,
a man's own nature speaks for itself.'

children.translated_text: With the word 'hi' (for), through the expression
of the meaning of a reason, to establish what has been said,
this <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s>
is made even more manifest, as:
'Mountains bear clouds
that have come, even though heavy;
for one who is greater indeed
bears the weighty who come with affection.'
When there is a demonstration of the distinction
of a meaning that has a standard of comparison,
they hold that to be <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast),
from the establishment of the distinction, as:
'Your eyes, dark and white
with eyelashes, with reddish lines —
but the lotus and the dark lily
are of unmixed white and dark.'
When there is the manifestation of a result
even in the denial of a cause —
that should be known as <s>vibhāvanā</s> (causation without cause),
concentration being easily attained, as:
'The peacocks have not drunk their fill; the quarters
are not agitated with longing;
the <s>nīpa</s> tree is not anointed with fragrance;
the water has not lost its muddiness.'
Where through what is said another meaning
is understood, having the same qualifier —
that is called <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression),
from the condensed nature of its meaning, as:
'Broad-shouldered, straight, without crookedness,
firm, bearing many great fruits,
this tree has grown tall
and was felled by the wind.'
Speech that, based on a cause,
transcends the scope of ordinary experience —
they consider that <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole),
as an ornament, as:
'By the radiance of its own flowers,
rivaling the moonbeams,
the <s>saptacchada</s> trees were found
only by the sound of swarming bees.'
'If the skin of water were loose
and could slough off like a serpent's skin,
then there would be white garments
on the limbs of women in the water.'
Thus has been stated
what arises from the conjunction of excellence in qualities;
but all <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole)
one should evaluate according to tradition.
All this is indeed <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression);
through it, meaning is made manifest.
The poet should exert effort in this;
what ornament exists without it?
Cause (<s>hetu</s>) and suggestion (<s>leśa</s>)
are not considered as ornaments,
because in the utterance of a combination
the oblique expression is not being expressed.
'The sun has set; the moon shines;
the birds go to their nests' —
such things — is this poetry?
They call this mere reportage.
<s>Yathāsaṃkhya</s> (enumeration in order) and <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy)
are known as two ornaments;
'enumeration,' O wise one,
has been stated elsewhere as <s>utprekṣā</s>.
Of many things indicated
that have dissimilar attributes,
the sequential description
is called <s>yathāsaṃkhya</s> (enumeration in order), as:
'By you are vanquished the lotus, moon, bee, elephant,
male cuckoo, and peacock,
by your face, beauty, eyes, gait,
voice, and hair.'
<s>Utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) does not intend a general similarity;
it has some affinity with simile,
and through the attribution of qualities or actions not its own,
it is endowed with excess.
'Under the guise of a <s>kiṃśuka</s> (flame-of-the-forest) tree,
climbing the tree on all sides,
fire seems to observe
the forests, both burnt and unburnt.'
Some declare that <s>svabhāvokti</s> (description of nature)
is an ornament;
the depiction of a thing in its true state
is called <s>svabhāva</s> (nature), as:
'Scolding, calling out to others,
running about in circles, crying,
the boy drives the cows
into the rice-fields with a stick.'
This has been stated in summary;
elaboration only wearies the intellect.
Whatever else has not been included
may be inferred in this direction.
This ornament of speech has been constructed by me
with examples made by myself.
Henceforth, another, manifold and charming,
method of verbal ornamentation shall be presented.
Thus ends the second chapter of <s>Bhāmaha</s>'s <s>Alaṅkāra</s>.
Third Chapter
<s>Preyas</s> (the appealing), <s>rasavat</s> (the rasa-imbued), <s>ūrjasvi</s> (the vigorous),
<s>paryāyokta</s> (the circumlocutory), <s>samāhita</s> (the well-composed),
<s>udātta</s> (the elevated) of two kinds,
and <s>śliṣṭa</s> (the punning) of three varieties —
<s>apahnuti</s> (denial), <s>viśeṣokta</s> (particular statement),
<s>virodha</s> (contradiction), <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal pairing),
<s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant),
and <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise) with illustration —
and another kind of <s>upamā-rūpaka</s> (simile-metaphor),
also <s>upameyopamā</s> (reciprocal simile),
<s>sahokti</s> (co-statement), <s>parivṛtti</s> (reversal),
with <s>saṃdeha</s> (doubt), <s>ananvaya</s> (self-comparison),
and <s>utprekṣāvayava</s> (part of poetic fancy),
others also <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination),
and <s>bhāvikatva</s> (dramaticness) — these ornaments
were proclaimed by the wise.
<s>Preyas</s> (the appealing): when <s>Kṛṣṇa</s> came to the house,
<s>Vidura</s> spoke as follows:
'Today, O <s>Govinda</s>,
the joy that has arisen in me at your arrival home
may in time
come again only from your visit.'

children.translated_text: <s>Rasavat</s> (rasa-imbued): where <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) and other
<s>rasas</s> (aesthetic sentiments) are clearly shown, as:
'The queen, at the time of union,
was hidden behind the ascetic's skin (<s>dharma-maskarin</s>).'
<s>Ūrjasvi</s> (the vigorous): as by <s>Karṇa</s>,
who returned to <s>Pārtha</s> (Arjuna) —
'Does <s>Karṇa</s> string the bow twice?'
'<s>Śalya</s>!' — thus the serpent was cast off.
<s>Paryāyokta</s> (the circumlocutory): when something is expressed
in an indirect manner, as:
'At the seizure of the jewels,
the bow <s>Śārṅga</s> spoke to the <s>Caidya</s> (Śiśupāla).'
'Whether in homes or on the road, we do not eat food
that has been studied over;
the twice-born do not eat that either,
in order to prevent the giving of flavors.'
<s>Samāhita</s> (the well-composed): in <s>Rājamitra</s>,
as with the <s>Kṣatriya</s> women —
'As the women went to greet <s>Rāma</s>,
<s>Nārada</s> appeared before them.'
<s>Udātta</s> (the elevated): '<s>Rāma</s>, mighty,
obedient to his teacher's words,
having renounced the kingdom that came to him,
went to the forest.'
Others, however, understand this differently
with a different explanation;
that which is endowed with various gems and the like
is called <s>udātta</s> (the elevated).
'<s>Cāṇakya</s>, entering at night
a pleasure-house set in darkness,
covered with moonstones,
recognized it by drops of water.'
When the nature of the subject of comparison
is established through the standard of comparison,
by quality, action, or name,
it is called <s>śliṣṭa</s> (the punning).
This is also the definition of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor);
certainly it is perceived here, but
the desired usage is the simultaneous application
of both standard and subject of comparison.

children.text: Could iṣṭaḥ be a corruption of śliṣṭaḥ ?

children.translated_text: 'Producing sprays, water, and ichor,
lofty — the cloud-elephants!'
Here, the description of clouds and elephants
is made simultaneously.
From punning (<s>śleṣa</s>), its division
into meaning and expression is made;
through co-statement, simile, or cause,
it is of three kinds, as:
'Shady, with serpents removed, with good riders,
fruit-giving —
the roadside trees, large,
exist for the welfare of others.'
'Elevated, beloved of the world,
great, abundantly raining,
they cool the earth's heat —
good kings are like clouds.'
'Because of possessing gems, because of unfathomable depth,
because of not transgressing one's own boundaries,
because of being the refuge of many creatures —
you are similar to the ocean.'
<s>Apahnuti</s> (denial) is also a desired figure,
somewhat containing simile within;
through the concealment of a real fact,
its designation is made, as:
'This is not a swarm of bees
buzzing loudly in intoxication again and again —
this is the sound of the bow
of <s>Kandarpa</s> (the god of love) being drawn.'
When, upon the removal of one aspect,
another quality is established —
for the purpose of showing the distinction,
that is regarded as <s>viśeṣokti</s> (particular statement), as:
'He alone, the flower-weaponed (<s>Kusumāyudha</s>, i.e. <s>Kāma</s>), conquers
the three worlds;
even when his body was destroyed
by <s>Śambhu</s> (Śiva), his power was not taken.'
When there is an attribution of a contradictory
action to a quality or to an action,
for the purpose of expressing a distinction —
the wise know that as <s>virodha</s> (contradiction).
By the grove growing up near the bank
Though cool as shade, that [fame] is fierce;
it torments your enemies
even from distant lands.
Even of one who is inferior, by the intention to express equality of qualities
with a superior one,
through the attribution of equal action and function—
this is called <s>tulyayogitā</s> (attribution of equal connection).
The rest is <s>Himagiri</s> (the Himālaya), and you—
both are great, venerable, and steadfast;
since both are of inviolable boundaries,
you both support the trembling earth.
The praise of another object that is not the subject under discussion
is called <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant),
and it is described
in the following manner:
Pleasing to the beloved, sweet,
ripened in due season, abundant,
without any human effort—
behold the fruit of the trees!
Under the pretext of praising one far superior in qualities,
the censure that actually intends
to establish equality to some degree—
that is <s>vyājastuti</s> (sarcastic praise), as follows:
<s>Rāma</s> split seven <s>sāla</s> trees,
<s>Bhṛgūttama</s> (Paraśurāma) split Mount <s>Krauñca</s>;
has even a hundredth part of what they did
been accomplished by you?
When a thing distinguished by its very action
is shown for the purpose of illustrating that meaning,
this is known as <s>nidarśanā</s> (exemplification),
without the use of particles like 'as if' or 'like'.
This sun of feeble radiance
wishes to proceed toward setting—
"rising leads to fall"—
thus awakening people regarding the fortunate.
When one establishes the nature of the subject of comparison
through the standard of comparison,
and states it as a simile—this
is <s>upamārūpaka</s> (simile-metaphor), as follows:
The measuring rod of the entire expanse of the sky—
the foot of <s>Viṣṇu</s> (the discus-bearer) triumphs!
It is a new mirror
for the moon-face of the celestial woman.

children.text: Is it that the foot is first "compared" to a measuring rod and then with a mirror for the faces of the celestial women that makes this upamārūpaka? \edM\ also puzzled.

children.translated_text: Where the roles of standard and subject of comparison
are alternated in turns,
that is called <s>upameyopamā</s> (reciprocal simile),
as stated here:
Fragrant, delighting the eyes,
flushed pink with the intoxication of wine—
your face is like a lotus,
and the lotus is like your face.
Where two simultaneous actions relating to two objects
are expressed
by a single word—
that is considered <s>sahokti</s> (co-expression), as follows:
With directions made turbid by falling snow,
causing tight embraces,
the nights grow longer,
along with the pleasures of lovers.
When the specification of a distinguished object
is made by the exclusion of other things,
that figure possessing <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroborative reasoning)
is called <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange), as follows:
Having given wealth to supplicants,
he obtained the wealth of fame;
of the virtuous who are universal benefactors,
this is the unfailing vow.
When one states both the identity
and the difference through a standard of comparison,
that utterance of deliberate doubt for the purpose of praise
is known as <s>sasandeha</s> (the doubtful), as follows:

children.text: kimayaṃ śaśī na sa divā virājate
children.translated_text: Is this the moon? No, it does not shine by day.
<s>Kusumāyudha</s> (the flower-armed Kāma)? No, his bow is not made of flowers.
Thus, even as I examine in wonder, my mind,
gazing upon you, cannot reach a definite conclusion.
Where that very thing serves as both
the standard and the subject of comparison,
with the intention of expressing incomparability—
that they call <s>ananvaya</s> (non-correlation).
With lips reddened by <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel),
with gleaming lustre of teeth,
with eyes resembling blue lotuses—
your face is like your face alone.
Connected with the meaning of a <s>śliṣṭa</s> (pun),
somewhat endowed with fancy,
and again with the sense of metaphor—
this is a component of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy), as follows:
Since its rising and setting are alike,
when the sun has gone toward setting,
the day, wearied,
seems to enter the house of darkness for rest.
The best ornament is <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination),
from the conjunction of many figures,
fashioned like a garland of gems—
and it is described as follows:
Of you two, both possessing depth and grace,
both abounding in jewels—
you are a delight for people to approach,
while the lord of waters harbours dangerous crocodiles.
Your face, of lotus-like radiance,
is beautiful without adornment;
for what is naturally charming,
what need is there of ornament?

children.text: [---thus saṃsṛṣṭi of vibhāvanā, upamā and arthāntaranyāsa]

children.translated_text: The combination of other figures too should be made
in this same manner;
how much can I explain
to those who understand subtleties?
<s>Bhāvikatva</s> (vividness) is called a quality
pertaining to the whole composition,
where past and future events
appear as if directly perceived.
Striking, exalted, and wondrous subject matter,
skilful construction of the narrative,
and clarity of diction—
these they declare to be its causes.

children.translated_text: <s>Āśīḥ</s> (benediction) too is regarded by some
as a figure of speech;
it is used in expressing good wishes
without contradicting friendship, as follows:
Abandon jealousy born of affection toward this friend;
embrace him tightly with honour, laying aside your pride;
like a great cloud raining upon Mount <s>Vindhya</s> in due season,
may he drench you with tears of joy from his eyes.
With <s>sāla</s> trees shattered by rut-maddened elephants,
with heroes slain, with citizens fleeing in terror,
with all splendour burnt by your valour—
may the assembly of kings behold the cities of their foes thus!
The system of figures of speech has been set forth in full,
determined by my own intellect and declared;
by this, the speech of those who know word and meaning is adorned,
and shines like a woman skilfully ornamented.
Thus ends the third chapter of <s>Bhāmaha</s>'s <s>Alaṃkāra</s>.
Fourth Chapter.
<s>Apārtha</s> (meaningless), <s>vyartha</s> (contradictory), <s>ekārtha</s> (tautologous),
<s>sasaṃśaya</s> (ambiguous), <s>apakrama</s> (disordered),
<s>śabdahīna</s> (grammatically deficient), <s>yatibhraṣṭa</s> (faulty in caesura),
<s>bhinnavṛtta</s> (metrically broken), and <s>visandhi</s> (faulty in euphonic combination),
and that which contradicts place, time, art,
common sense, logic, and scripture,
and that which is deficient in thesis, reason,
or example, or is fallacious—these are not approved.
<s>Apārtha</s> means devoid of meaning;
and meaning belongs to both word and sentence.
A meaningful combination of phonemes
ending in a nominal or verbal suffix is a word;
a combination of words
that are mutually expectant,
and that sentence is one which, being complete in sense,
is bound to a single topic.
In phonemes that occur in sequence,
combination and the like cannot apply;
but in the mind this is possible
at every moment, even though they are different.
The cognition, whose object is the final sound,
carries the memory imparted by the preceding phonemes—
this is what some call the sentence,
not the sounds themselves, which are momentarily perishing.
Much more could be said on this topic,
but that has not been stated here;
why engage in dispute with the masters?
Let us return to the subject at hand.
That which is devoid of collective meaning
is considered <s>apārthaka</s> (meaningless),
such as: 'ten pomegranates, six cakes'—
and so on, as stated.
<s>Vyartha</s> (contradictory) is considered to be self-contradictory in meaning;
contradiction is indicated
when earlier and later meanings conflict,
producing a reversal, as follows:
"Friend, show pride toward your beloved,
do not accept a lowly position;"
yet: "Women who follow their husband's wishes
do not destroy love."
"You, having attained greatness through serving your elders,
with senses and enemies conquered,
the very foundation of welfare through discipline—
now simply stand firm."
When meanings are not different from each other,
that is called <s>ekārtha</s> (tautology);
others call this repetition,
distinguishing by word and meaning.
Verbal repetition, however, is not described here
due to its obviousness;
how could one whose mind is engaged
repeat what has already been said?
In cases of fear, grief, envy,
joy, and wonder,
as when one says 'go, go!'—
that is not considered repetition by the learned.
Here, what constitutes repetition of meaning
is itself considered <s>ekārtha</s> (tautology),
as when restating what has been said,
since no purpose is served, as follows:
Surely the sound of waters makes her
restless with longing—
those waters released from the clouds,
falling from the mouths of drainpipes on the mansions.
From hearing common properties
without a particular being specified,
the knowledge that is unsettled in this regard—
that the learned call <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt).

children.translated_text: That speech which generates such doubt
is called <s>sasaṃśaya</s> (the doubtful);
a statement intended for certainty
should not waver, as follows:
Infested with serpents, difficult to climb,
rich in gems, bearing fruit,
uneven are the mountains—from them
danger swiftly comes to the careless.
The order prescribed according to instruction
is considered the proper sequence here;
what deviates from that through transposition
is called <s>apakrama</s> (disorder).
Wearing crescent moons as diadems,
dark-cloud-hued and snow-white,
bearing the discus and the trident—
may <s>Śambhu</s> and <s>Śārṅgin</s> (Viṣṇu) protect you!
When usage deviates from the prescriptions of the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (grammarian),
commentators, and approved practice,
and cannot be established by the authority of trustworthy speakers—
that the learned call <s>śabdahīna</s> (grammatically deficient), as follows:
Girdled with flashing lightning,
swelling with vast masses of water,
obscuring the radiance of the sun—
behold the clouds all around the sky!

children.text: Why is this śabdahīna? Is it perhaps that we have an -in suffix attached to what could be a bahuvrīhi (sphurattaḍidvalayinaḥ)?

children.translated_text: <s>Yati</s> (caesura) is the examination of words
that have been fitted into a metre;
what deviates from that is called <s>yatibhraṣṭa</s> (faulty in caesura),
as indicated here:
These rain-clouds, dark-bodied as <s>tamāla</s> trees, girded with lightning, thunder!

children.text: This pāda of sragdharā lacks the yati after the first seven syllables (sragdharā should have a caesura after each group of 7 syllables).

children.translated_text: When a heavy or light syllable
is placed in the wrong position in composition,
or when there is a deficiency or excess thereof—
that is <s>bhinnavṛtta</s> (broken metre), as follows:
The swarm of bees wanders intoxicated through the forests!
"Bereft of your beloved, you should indeed depart now."

children.text: line 2: a pāda of kṣmā (not to be confused with kṣamā), according to Apte's "A Classified List of Sanskrit Dictionaries" (Appendix A, Part II).

children.translated_text: When the beloved <s>Śambhu</s>, whose crest-jewel is the moon,
takes up the rays of the moon—
may <s>Śambhu</s> and <s>Śarvāṇī</s> (Pārvatī) protect you!—
thus they declare an example of <s>visandhi</s> (faulty juncture).
When the occurrence of a substance in a place
is not attested or is impossible,
that should be understood as a violation
of nature itself, as stated here:
On <s>Malaya</s>, near the slopes of caves,
where <s>kālāguru</s> (black aloe) trees have grown,
bowing with fragrant blossoms,
the <s>devadāru</s> (deodar) trees shine.
Time is divided sixfold
according to the distinction of six seasons;
that which violates this—they say—
is a fault of temporal inconsistency, as follows:
Though the winds blow bearing heavy showers of frost,
as in the rainy season,
these mango trees adorning the forest
bloom and spread their fragrance.
<s>Kalā</s> (art) includes enumeration, intelligence,
crafts, and related domains;
what is presented in a confused manner
is likewise declared to violate these, as follows:
From <s>ṛṣabha</s>, the fifth note,
is known as <s>dhaivata</s> together with <s>ṣaḍja</s>;
this is the <s>madhyama-grāma</s> (middle scale),
in which <s>ṛṣabha</s> is flattened.
Thus what is presented as established
is understood quite differently due to confusion;
in other arts as well,
such violation should be pointed out.
Those who know reality distinguish the world
into the stationary and the moving;
and the conventions regarding these—
what violates them is a fault, as follows:
From the drops of rut-fluid
falling from the temple-ridges of their elephants,
a terrible river arose,
carrying horses, elephants, and chariots.
From the mouths of the running army-steeds,
froth and water that fell
created knee-deep pools of drink
in every direction of the roads.
<s>Nyāya</s> (logic) refers to the science of governance,
discourse on the three aims, and statecraft;
what violates logic—they hold—
is that which departs from it, as follows:
Having introduced the king of <s>Vatsa</s>,
who was desirous of conquest and guided by elder counsel,
the author then ascribed to that very able king
a lack of intelligence-gathering.
The elephant-stratagem filled inside
with hundreds of warriors, led by <s>Sālaṅkāyana</s>—
such a device entering his own territory
he did not recognize.
Or if it was overlooked by his ministers
for achieving their own ends,
then alas, what dullness was theirs!
Or is there no loyalty to their lord?
Arrows released from the strong bows
of wrathful enemies—
that they would avoid his vital parts
and fall elsewhere—who could assume this?
"He killed my brother,
my son, my father,
my maternal uncle, my nephew"—
with minds inflamed by fury,
hurling various weapons in battle
at one who was helpless,
alone and in an unfamiliar forest—
how could many not slay him?
Homage to those learned ones
who, understanding this intention of the poet,
setting aside the standards of science and common practice,
guide it thus, being versed in policy!
Even a child knows the difference
between a living elephant
and one made of hide—

children.text: kaṣṭaṃ kiṃ nu kathaṃ nu tat
children.translated_text: how strange! How could that be?
<s>Āgama</s> (scripture) refers to the <s>dharmaśāstras</s>
and the social boundaries established by them;
what violates them through transgression
of their customs, as follows:
Of kings who had drunk <s>Soma</s>,
who stood on the righteous path,
in a lineage one wished to adorn,
with an elder present, though desirous of conquest—
<s>Naravāhanadatta</s>, a twice-born
who had not married and was without
the proper sacraments,
was afflicted by courtesans at night.
This rule has not been cited for the purpose of censure,
nor out of arrogance—what then, for understanding?
For who among people like me would detect
hidden intentions in the work of self-realized seers of truth?
Thus ends the fourth chapter of <s>Bhāmaha</s>'s <s>Alaṃkāra</s>.
Fifth Chapter.
Now, that which is deficient in <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis), <s>hetu</s> (reason), and the rest,
as well as that which is fallacious, is described
briefly, in accordance with logic,
for the understanding of just that much.
Generally, due to the difficulty of comprehension,
the dull-witted shrink from the science of logic;
to entice them, this
is a small collection of logical reasoning.
Even the science of logic is employed
when mixed with the sweet <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic flavour) of poetry;
those who first taste honey
then drink bitter medicine.
There is no word, no object of expression,

children.text: na sa nyāyo na sā kalā
children.translated_text: no logical principle, no art
that does not become a component of poetry—
ah, how great is the burden of the poet!
<s>Sattva</s> and the other categories are known through two means of knowledge:
<s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference);
the domain of unique particulars and universals
belongs to these two respectively.
<s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is free from conceptual construction;
then from that object [arises inference]—so say some;
they hold that conceptual construction means
the attribution of name, class, and so forth.
The superimposition is just this much,
and that [cognition] has a real object as its support.
Where is the function in the exclusion of universal and the like?
Where is the particular, and whence does it come?
And in the exclusions of those,
that [exclusion] is likewise established as the domain of the intellect.
If [it is] without substance and thus false,
perception would function in accord with reality indeed.
If it is held that by the division of apprehended and apprehender,
[it is] a portion of consciousness,
then due to its mere similarity to consciousness,
its particular [nature] is [merely] conceptual construction.
'From the object itself' — thus from form and the like,
'from that alone' and 'not from anything else';
otherwise, the cognition of a pot
would be designated by another [name].
Some [hold that] knowledge from a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) possessing three characteristics
is inference (<s>anumāna</s>);
others know it as the perception of that which is
inseparably connected with one who knows it.
The subject (<s>dharmin</s>), qualified by the property under dispute,
made specific [thereby],
is the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>); and the statement of that
is called the proposition (<s>pratijñā</s>).
One that contradicts the purpose of that [thesis], the reason,
the established doctrine, or all scriptures,
that has a well-known property, and that is contradicted
by perception — [such a proposition] is faulty.
For by that [proposition] itself, the contradiction
of that purpose is effected, as in:
'My father is an ascetic from childhood,'
['and I am] the legitimate son of whom.'
'The self exists' or 'Nature (<s>Prakṛti</s>) exists' —
such [a proposition] should be known as one that contradicts the reason,
since the subject [itself] is not established,
the property of that [subject] will also not be established.
When, regarding the well-established subject of sound,
'it is eternal' or 'it is non-eternal' —
a dispute arises between debaters
concerning the [specific] difference.
One that contradicts one's own established doctrine should be known
as contradicting that [doctrine];
as when <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> (Kaṇāda) were to declare
sound to be imperishable.
One contradicting all scriptures
[is] due to contradicting all teachings;
as [the claim]: 'The body is pure,' or 'there are three
means of knowledge, or there are none.'

children.text: śucastanustrīṇi pramāṇāni na santi vā] \edM\edBGa; śucistanuḥ straiṇī tatpramāṇāni santi vā \edB; śuci * sunu straiṇī \lac \GnoliMS

children.translated_text: One having a well-known property — one qualified by
a property that is undoubted from childhood —
is considered [a proposition] with an established property;
as [the statement] 'sound is apprehended by the ear.'
One contradicted by perception
is refuted by that very means of knowledge;
as: 'Fire is cold,' 'there is no form,'
'the moon is hot.'
Present in both [the similar and dissimilar cases], established as the same,
and excluded from the opposite of that —
the reason with three characteristics should be known;
a pseudo-reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) [arises] from the reverse.
'Present in both' means that which is established
in both one's own thesis and the opponent's thesis;
[this] thesis, having an undifferentiated characteristic,
is twofold by the difference of result.
When the opponent's thesis is not adopted
and the occurrence of that [reason] in it is not illustrated,
how can the establishment of the pseudo-reason
of 'unestablished in one [side]' be maintained?
That which, from the agreement with the property to be proved,
is similar [to the locus] and present there —
even though it is something else, that one, as if identical,
is figuratively referred to based on the universal.
The dissimilar case is that which is unlike it,
from which [the reason] is excluded, being absent there.
Thus, the agreement with both and
the exclusion are the marks of a good [reason].

children.text: Purport: anugati and vyāvṛtti are required respectively in 2 things (viz. pakṣa and sapakṣa) and in 1 thing (viz. vipakṣa).

children.translated_text: An example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) is said to be one established
by both the property to be proved and the proving property;
its counterpart is from the reverse;
a pseudo-example [arises] from its non-occurrence.
That by which the agreement of the mark with the provable
and its non-existence in the absence [of the provable]
is made known — that example
is said by others to be of two kinds.
Refutation (<s>dūṣaṇa</s>) is the argument of deficiency and the like;
deficient by reason and the like, or —
since the discourse is rooted in that —
deficient in the proposition is undesirable.

children.text: hetvādinātha vā] \edM; hetvādinātra ca \edB; hetvādinātha ca \edBGa

children.translated_text: The <s>jāti</s>s (futile rejoinders) are pseudo-refutations;
they are [types like] 'similarity' and so on.
Their elaboration in many ways
is not stated here due to prolixity.
Hereafter, the characteristics of reasoning
as applied in poetry will be stated.
But this [logic] as contained within treatise-like
poems has been described as follows.
Now, a cause is observed in the world
as that which is eternally inseparable [from its effect].
If it is a cause, it is not eternal;
if it is eternal, it is not a cause.
The mark of faults in application
is set forth in the treatises in another way,
through this kind of differentiation,
for the establishment of <s>sandhi</s> (treaty) and the like.
By the experts, in poetic applications,
that has been manifested differently.
There, poetry relies on the world,
[while] scriptures [rely on] those who see the truth.
'The sky is like a sword,
sound is one that follows from afar;
the water of rivers is perpetual —
oh, the stability of the great flame!'
Just as a substance, the support of form and the like,
perishes — so too [does its support].
They assert a proposition (<s>pratijñā</s>)
that is the acceptance of the desired conclusion.
Based on <s>dharma</s> (duty), <s>artha</s> (wealth), <s>kāma</s> (desire), and anger,
that [proposition] is fourfold.
'I will bear the old age of this one [my father]' —
having made such a promise to his father,
like <s>Puruṇā</s> (Pūru), who bore [his father's old age] —
that would be one grounded in <s>dharma</s>.
'I will find <s>Sītā</s> myself' —
thus, at the command of the husband,
having made a promise, by <s>Hanumān</s>,
she was found — that is one grounded in <s>artha</s> (purpose).
'I will carry away today this daughter
of <s>Mahāsena</s> (Skanda)' —
having made this promise, by <s>Vatsa</s>
she was carried away — that is one grounded in desire (<s>kāma</s>).
'Having crushed my brother's enemy,
I will drink his blood in battle' —
having made this promise, <s>Bhīma</s>
did exactly that, compelled by wrath.
The application should be made nowhere else
than in the proposition, under any circumstances;
and the abandonment of any
of these four should not be done.
As when <s>Suyodhana</s> (Duryodhana), having vowed
to fast unto death,
rose again for the kingdom —
that is [an example of] one contradicting <s>dharma</s>.
'When challenged, I will not turn back
from a game of dice' — [said] <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>;
having made an agreement with <s>Śakuni</s>,
he gambled — that is one detrimental to <s>artha</s> (purpose).
'From today I shall dwell
like a sage, by [my father's] word' —
that [vow] which <s>Bhīṣma</s> made for the sake
of his father — that was one detrimental to desire (<s>kāma</s>).
As <s>Rāma</s> made renounce
the vow concerning the slaughter of all <s>kṣatriya</s>s,
having defeated <s>Jāmadagnya</s> (<s>Paraśurāma</s>) in battle —
that should be known as one overcoming anger.
Next, the attainment of the accepted conclusion
without [formal] acceptance of a treaty (<s>sandhi</s>);
where even what is unstated is said to be
accepted from the [force of the] meaning.
'What is to be known by one hostile to the senses?
Who is subdued by enemies?
Who, being swift, does not give
wealth to supplicants promptly?'
The objection 'why?' [in this context]
shows the ease [of the conclusion].
The reason with three characteristics alone is accepted
even in poetry by the wise.
For positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) and negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>)
are sufficient by themselves for establishing the meaning;
as: 'On all sides of the forest expanse
there is this great lake —
[known] from the cooing of female ospreys
and from the fragrance of lotuses.'
Even a property belonging to another [subject] establishes that,
through its connection,
like the inference of fire in a region
from smoke rising to the sky.
And here a reason is perceived even when the provable
is not separately stated,
as when the understanding of meaning [proceeds]
without [explicit] positive and negative concomitance.
Night arose, needing lamps;
with the departure of the sun.
The reason is the need for lamps,
upon the departure of the sun, here.
For that [reason] too, the wise desire
the three faults previously mentioned —
as when produced by ignorance, doubt,
and erroneous cognition, for instance:
'These <s>kāśa</s> grasses captivate the heart
through the fragrance of flowers;
from their proximity to water
they should be known as arrow-reeds.'
'That one, from having white tips to its eyes,
should be taken as a <s>cakora</s> bird;
since it has not been seen in a similar species,
let it establish its <s>cakora</s>-ness.'
An illustration (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) of a stated meaning
is a display of a reflected image.
'Let it rather be a simile-inference' —
no, because of the non-statement of the reason.
The statement of the provable and the prover
is not desired elsewhere than where stated;
in 'the face is like a lotus' —
what is the provable and what is the prover?
Thus, just as [logic] in application exists
even in art —
'one is better by being taught by elders,
as in the first <s>Kṛta</s> age.'
Where the provable and the prover
are suggested by the example alone,
they call that a pure example;
since it is revealed by that alone, as in:
'You are <s>Bharata</s>, you are <s>Dilīpa</s>,
you are <s>Aila</s> <s>Purūravas</s>,
you are, O hero, <s>Pradyumna</s> himself,
you are <s>Naravāhana</s> himself.'
'How could his virtues
be expressed in a single word?' —
thus some good [poets] employ [verses],
some being afraid of prolixity.
A single word that is excellent [is better than] a good [poem]
that does not rely on recent composition;
from reversal, that [poor word]
effects the reversal even of fame.
Unpleasing, without clear meaning,
lacking charm even though having <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic essence) —
such poetry is like an unripe wood-apple;
like that of some [poets], for instance:

children.text: kapitthamāmaṃ yat keṣāṃcittādṛśaṃ] \edM; kapitthamāmraṃ vat(maṃca) keṣāñcitsadṛśaṃ \edB

children.translated_text: 'Of him whose feet are worshipped by the best of people, the foremost among kings,
who is the abode of great fame, long honored,
the son of the serpent-slayer, the lotus-born, who dwells in the water-enemy [the sun] —
of him alone, not of another son, is this conduct.'
With radiant jewels
and with trees laden with fruit,
and with blossoming flowers — others
adorn their speech, as [in the verse]:
'On the summit of <s>Sumeru</s>, variegated with fine emeralds and rubies,
with fruitful trees of many lovely leaves,
adorned with abundant flowers,
thronged with gods, sages, and <s>siddha</s>s — there he stood.'
By these constituents — ornaments, gardens, garlands —
speech is adorned.
The expression of indirect meaning and sound in speech
serves as ornamentation (<s>alaṃkāra</s>).
Others make poetry with contradictory words,
meaningless, full of padding, confused —
from the desire for prolixity,
as [in the verse]:
'Rich with <s>elātaka</s>, <s>kola</s>, <s>nāga</s>, <s>sphuṭa</s>, <s>bakula</s> creepers, sandalwood, and <s>spandana</s>,
its shores pervaded by pearls, camphor, <s>cakra</s>, aloe, <s>manasśilā</s>, and <s>sthāsaka</s>,
crowded within by hosts of conches, filled with swarms of fish and <s>makara</s>s, its waves spreading,
the ocean bore a fame pure as moonlight, <s>kumuda</s> flowers, ambrosia, and milk.'
Thus these ornaments of speech have been described by me,
having examined the manifold compositions of others and having reflected upon them myself.
The good, whose words are renowned, are authorities here; others [must judge] —
the mind of those of greater intellect is not easily won by those of untrained understanding.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of <s>Bhāmaha</s>'s <s>Alaṃkāra</s>.
Sixth Chapter
Having [the depth of] the ocean of <s>sūtra</s>s (aphorisms), with eddies of words,
with the depth of recitation,
with schools of verbal roots, <s>uṇādi</s> [suffixes], and <s>gaṇa</s>s (classes),
with the great raft of meditation-planets,
whose extent is surveyed by the wise,
envied by the foolish,
always enjoyed by all
the ray-particles of other sciences,
without crossing this profound
ocean of grammar (<s>vyākaraṇa</s>),
this person is not able to attain
the jewel of words by himself.
One who desires to compose poetry
should make effort in the mastery of that [grammar];
what pleasure is there in that which is done
on the authority of another?
Speech dependent on the words of others
does not shine for the delight of the good,
[like] a garland of flowers released
by another — graceful though it be.
The primary rule is this:
that one operates by one's own power;
those called 'learned through others'
are merely repeaters of others' statements.
Some say the word is that
from which the understanding of meanings arises;
even the radiance of smoke would have attained
word-hood with respect to the inference of fire.
Indeed, the aggregate of phonemes like <s>a</s> and the like
has a referent;
proclaimed for the understanding of meaning,
it is called a 'word.'
How can an aggregate be meaningful
when the individual [phonemes] are incapable [of meaning]?
Since phonemes occur in sequence,
neither is there a simultaneous collection.
Nor does the aggregate differ
from its constituent parts;
beyond timber, walls, and floor —
what other house is conceived?
Therefore, the notion that [the word-unit] is unchanging (<s>kūṭastha</s>) —
this verbal construction of yours is futile.
Where perception or inference [applies],
that is the ultimate reality.
Even with oaths, the word
of the <s>sphoṭa</s>-theorists should not be accepted.
'A flower called <s>namaḥ</s> (obeisance) exists' —
what sentient being would believe that?
Such are the phonemes, up to this extent,
denoting such-and-such meanings;
for the practical usage of the world,
a convention was made thus in the beginning.
That [word] is said to be unchanging, imperishable,
and nothing other than <s>nāda</s> (sound);
the dull-witted consider conventional meanings
to be ultimate realities.
Whether perishable or eternal,
or connected with an existing object,
obeisance to those learned ones
who are the authority for its determination!
Others declare that a word conveys its meaning
through the exclusion of others (<s>anyāpoha</s>);
and <s>anyāpoha</s> is indeed nothing but
the negation of other categories.
If the word 'cow' achieves its purpose
in the exclusion of others,
let another sound be sought
that generates the cognition of a cow in [the object] cow.
Words have the understanding of meaning as their result,
and a single [word] does not have a double result;
how then, for you, can one [word] have
both exception and rule as results?
Previously, the cognition 'cow' would arise
from hearing the word 'cow';
by which [convention], for the purpose of negating 'non-cow,'
the sound 'cow' was employed.
This is differentiated by the difference of phonemes;
phonemes [are differentiated] by the conception of their own parts.
What are words? What is their denotation?
Oh, this is a path difficult to traverse!
Those [words] are also fourfold by the distinction of
substance, action, universal, and quality;
others also accept an arbitrary word (<s>yādṛcchā-śabda</s>)
such as <s>Ḍittha</s> and the like.
Of those [words] that range over different languages
and whose objects are unlimited —
by what specific criterion
is their extent determined?
Those [words] that are correct in the usage
of poets with indirect speech,
and those that are not fit to be used —
this discrimination is now stated.
One should not use an unused [word]
that causes confusion of the mind;
for even with the same meaning, who would use
'<s>hanti</s>' (to kill) as a word denoting motion?
But one derived from Vedic [usage], though not easily understood —
[one should] not [use what begins with] <s>duṣṭa</s> and the like, which is inelegant,
nor what is vulgar, like [words beginning with] <s>piṇḍī</s>, <s>śūra</s>, and the like,
nor what is meaningless, like [words beginning with] <s>ḍittha</s> and the like.
One should not [employ] unfamiliar or otherwise-meaning [words],
due to the multiplicity of meanings of verbal roots;
nor [use words] drawn by [mere] hint of suggestion,
as in 'he kills' or 'he meditates' [used ambiguously].
One should not [use a word] merely because it was used by the learned,
nor what is established in another [grammatical] system;
and saying 'it is like the Vedic [usage],' by the general rule,
one should also not utter a Vedic form [in secular poetry].
One should employ a word that is received by tradition, pleasant to the ear,
and meaningful;
for the beauty of expression surpasses
any other ornament.
One that is established through supplementary enumeration,
and one that is derived by the <s>iṣṭi</s> (desired interpretation) —
one should generally prefer those,
but not what arises from the division of grammatical operation.
This maiden is moon-faced,
captivating by her very nature;
a golden ornament on her
greatly nourishes her beauty.
One should employ the form showing augmentation,
as in the case of the root <s>mṛj</s> (to wipe) with <s>saṃkrama</s> also;
'Those falling teardrops wipe away
the redness of her lower lip.'
But in <s>ekaśeṣa</s> (single remainder), where the masculine
is retained with a feminine —
as stated: '<s>Varuṇa</s> and <s>Indra</s>,
the two <s>Bhava</s>s, the two <s>Śarva</s>s, the two <s>Mṛḍa</s>s.'
As in '<s>paṭayati</s>' (he causes to weave) and the like,
the causative from the nominal base, therefore;
and by the <s>iṣṭi</s> of [the usage] 'as if <s>ṇāviṣṭhavat</s>,
likewise '<s>kraśayati</s>' (he causes to become thin).
One should employ the <s>avyayībhāva</s> (indeclinable compound)
ending in a short vowel, and not as the fifth [case];
in the view of the third and seventh [cases],
one should not bring [usage] into the domain of <s>aluk</s>.
In <s>tiṣṭhadgu</s> and the like, [these forms] are to be used
in the sphere of night and day;
as in 'the learned one studies',
'<s>tiṣṭhadgu</s>' and '<s>vahadgu</s>'.
By the mere usage of the learned alone,
or by the opinion of the author of the <s>Nyāsa</s>,
one should not in any way cite [a form]
having a combined genitive with the <s>tṛc</s> suffix.
By the mere indicatory power (<s>jñāpaka</s>) of the <s>sūtra</s>,
as '<s>Vṛtrahantā</s>' is cited —
one should not form a construction with '<s>aka</s>'
as it conveys [the meaning in that way].
'<s>Pañcarājī</s>' — thus, for example,
one should employ the <s>dvigu</s> compound in the feminine;
the neuter <s>tatpuruṣa</s> [compound],
as in '<s>puruhūtasabham</s>'.
From all [roots] like <s>bhṛśa</s> and the like,
one should speak with the final consonant dropped, as in:
'She becomes proud for you, O beloved one —
why do you, O deceitful one, become conceited?'
The third [person] singular in the genitive,
and the vocative form in the <s>kvip</s> suffix —
as stated: 'By the slayer of <s>Bala</s>,
of the radiances, like lightnings.'
Even a sentence that is not [attested],
one should employ it just as it is;
as it is said: '<s>ambhasā bhāsā</s>,
<s>yaśasām ambhasām</s>'.
In masculine and feminine, the <s>kvasU</s>-ending form
they desire as non-Vedic, indeed;
'Even of those who have attained heaven,
the beauty does not depart' — as shown.
The maiden, wearing a bodice over her breasts
that resemble the frontal globes of an elephant,
exhausted by the fatigue of lovemaking,
stole the hearts of men.

children.text: kañcukaṃ stane] \edM; kantuke stanau \edB; kantukau stanau \edBGha

children.translated_text: From <s>śabala</s> and the like, the causative (<s>ṇij</s>)
shines especially well, as in:
'O fair-waisted one, behold the herons!
They are making the clouds spotted.'
Resembling the droplets of a cool shower,
the <s>setu-gandhavāṭ</s> (bridge-garden breeze)
fans you, O fair-waisted one,
whose eyes are languid from the weariness of lovemaking.
Thus the usage of the causative (<s>ṇic</s>) is always
the supreme ornament;
and the <s>ṇini</s> suffix, applicable in all three genders,
in the domain of habitual action —
'Her bosom is charming,
her face is beautiful and charming,
her body is exceedingly charming —
how much does it not steal the mind!'
In [the sense of] habitual action and the like,
all [suffixes] like <s>tṛn</s> and the like are desired;
and especially preferred therein
are <s>yuc</s>, <s>kurac</s>, <s>jvara</s>, <s>jiṣṇuc</s> [sic].
One should also employ the <s>ktin</s>-ending [form],
such as <s>saṃgati</s> (conjunction), <s>saṃhati</s> (compactness);
and the forms with the <s>śa</s> affix, and <s>jāguriṣṭau</s>,
as in <s>jāgaryā</s>, <s>jāgarā</s>.
And '<s>upāsanā</s>' — one should always employ
the <s>yuc</s> suffix from the root <s>ās</s>;
and the <s>lyuṭ</s> suffix in the agent sense,
as in <s>devana</s> (one who plays), <s>ramaṇa</s> (one who delights).
The feminine suffix <s>ṅīp</s> is preferred also after <s>aṇ</s>-ending [words],
as <s>Lakṣmī</s>, <s>Paurandarī</s>;
from <s>mahārājan</s> [comes] <s>lākṣā</s> (lac),
and <s>ṭhak</s> likewise from <s>rocanā</s> (yellow pigment).
The <s>ḍmatup</s>-preferred [form] from <s>kumuda</s> (water lily),
as in 'this earth is <s>kumudvatī</s> (abounding in water lilies)';
and <s>ṭhak</s> also with 'he conquers by that',
as <s>ākṣika</s> (dice-player), <s>śāstrika</s> (one versed in scripture).
In the section on what is beneficial, <s>ṇam</s>
is employed from the word <s>sarva</s>;
and from that, by the <s>iṣṭi</s> of <s>cham</s>, as in
'<s>sārva</s>' and '<s>sarvīya</s>'.
One should also use the <s>imanij</s>-ending [form],
as <s>paṭimā</s> (sharpness), <s>laghimā</s> (lightness);
and especially the <s>īyasun</s>-ending one —
'The elder one approached the younger one.'
The <s>dvayasaj</s> and <s>daghnac</s> [suffixes] are preferred
in the domain of measurement, as in:
'The river-woman is knee-deep;
the lake is [deep as] two hips.'
In the section on <s>matup</s>, [we have] <s>jyotsnā</s> (moonlight),
<s>tamisrā</s> (dark night), <s>śṛṅgiṇ</s> (horned one), and the like;
and <s>ina</s> from <s>phala</s> (fruit) and <s>barha</s> (peacock tail),
as <s>phalin</s> (fruit-bearing), <s>barhiṇ</s> (peacock).
<s>Ini</s> is generally employed
as well as <s>ṭham</s> by the wise;
therein especially <s>mekhalā</s> (girdle), <s>mālā</s> (garland),
<s>māyā</s> (illusion) and the like are considered.
From the reduplicated [root], in the <s>jhe</s> replacement,
'<s>dadhatī</s>' and the like also;
'<s>roditi</s>' (he weeps), '<s>svapiti</s>' (he sleeps) and the like —
with <s>iṭ</s>, is the whole-root (<s>sārvadhātuka</s>) [suffix].
In reduplicated [forms], the <s>a</s>-ending
of <s>śatṛ</s> from <s>ghu</s> and <s>bhṛñ</s> should be employed;
'She, wearing (<s>dadhat</s>) an ornament,
and bearing (<s>bibhrat</s>) a garland, shines.'
[One should not, with the letter <s>śa</s>,]
ever pronounce a conjunct of the <s>ta</s>-class;
as in: 'This dark forest shines,
O lotus-eyed one.'

children.translated_text: One should not [use] an excessive [repetition of] the letter <s>a</s> in one place,
as in <s>gata</s>, <s>yāta</s>, <s>hata</s>;
except for assimilation, <s>ha</s> for <s>jha</s>
one should use, and not otherwise than by convention.
This [system] of <s>Śālāturīya</s> (<s>Pāṇini</s>) is endless in sequence —
'Who will expound it?' — therefore I cease this investigation;
if anyone reaches the far shore of the ocean of words,
and of the fearsome-watered sea — that would be the wonder!
It is the constant resort of all other sciences,
and does not obstruct any meanings stated in them;
the <s>Pāṇinīya</s> system is to be revered in the world,
yet through neutrality, it is not the authority of anyone [in particular].
Having examined the views of the great poets,
and having understood the characteristics of poetry through one's own intellect,
for the instruction of the good, by <s>Bhāmaha</s>,
this [work] has been composed by the son of <s>Rakrilagomi</s>.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the illustrious <s>Kāvyālaṃkāra</s> of <s>Bhāmaha</s>.

children.translated_text: In sixty [verses], the body [of poetry] was determined;
in one hundred and sixty, the ornaments;
in fifty, the perception of faults;
in seventy, the determination of principles;
in sixty, the purity of words —
thus these five topics
have been stated in six chapters
by <s>Bhāmaha</s>, in order, for you.
